The Australian swamp rat (Rattus lutreolus) is a medium-sized murid rodent inhabiting dense riparian and heathland vegetation along the eastern coast of Australia. Females typically produce litters of five pups [N_R_i = litters of five pups] during the breeding season, and the maximum annual reproductive output has been estimated at approximately 2 to 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 litters per year] in populations occurring under a mean body temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. Reproductive activity is largely confined to spring and summer, when food resources become abundant and water availability is highest. The combination of moderate litter size and repeated breeding events across the warmer months likely represents an adaptive response to the unpredictability of wetland conditions in their coastal sedge and swamp habitats, where prey abundance can fluctuate substantially between years. This species exhibits a relatively slow life-history pace compared to other Rattus species of similar body mass. The interval between successive litters, coupled with the dependency period of the young, suggests that individual females can successfully rear only a limited number of offspring to independence within a single reproductive season, a pattern that is consistent with the demands of lactation in a cool, temperate environment.

This pubertal milestone is reached while the juvenile is still gaining mass and refining its foraging skills, and it represents the point at which the individual becomes physiologically capable of participating in the breeding population. The timing of this event is influenced by both nutritional condition and population density, with females in high-quality habitats maturing at the lower end of the range. The age at first reproduction, however, may be delayed beyond 79 days after birth [tR = 79 days after birth] if environmental conditions are unfavorable, as females must accumulate sufficient somatic reserves before investing in pregnancy and lactation. This flexibility in the onset of reproductive capacity is a common feature among small-bodied mammals inhabiting seasonally variable environments, and it allows females to adjust their life-history scheduling according to prevailing food availability and predation risk. The attainment of puberty at this moderate age is consistent with the species' overall strategy of slow growth and relatively late maturation compared to smaller, more fecund murids.

The gestation period in Rattus lutreolus lasts 27 days [tg = 27 days] when measured under standard physiological conditions at a core body temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C]. This interval encompasses the complete embryogenesis and foetal development phases, from the initial fertilisation of the ovum to the live birth of the altricial pups. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild is approximately 4.4 years [am = approximately 4.4 years] when measured under a mean body temperature of 36.7 °C [T = 36.7 °C], although many individuals succumb to predation or environmental stressors well before reaching this limit.
